source.title: Association of Upper Extremity Pain With Softball Pitching Kinematics and Kinetics

paper.citation: Oliver, G. D., Friesen, K., Barfield, J. W., Giordano, K., Anz, A., Dugas, J., & Andrews, J. (2019). Association of upper extremity pain with softball pitching kinematics and kinetics. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine, 7(8), 2325967119865171. https://doi.org/10.1177/2325967119865171
paper.abstract: Which lower-body/trunk kinematics and shoulder kinetics at foot contact are associated with self-reported upper-extremity pain in Division I softball pitchers? Thirty-seven NCAA Division I female pitchers: 13 with upper-extremity pain and 24 pain-free. Laboratory riseball pitching; only right-handed pitchers entered the modeled analysis. Directly relevant to collegiate softball, not overhand throwing or football. Descriptive cross-sectional laboratory study using electromagnetic tracking. Fastest of three strike-zone riseballs was analyzed. Backward-elimination regression considered 10 candidate variables with binary self-reported pain.
paper.tldr: This paper informs the boundary between mechanics associated with current pain and mechanics that prospectively cause injury. Stride length, trunk rotation, and center-of-mass position jointly explained adjusted R² = 0.33 of pain-group variance at foot contact. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Descriptive cross-sectional laboratory study using electromagnetic tracking. Fastest of three strike-zone riseballs was analyzed. Backward-elimination regression considered 10 candidate variables with binary self-reported pain.
paper.findings: Stride length, trunk rotation, and center-of-mass position jointly explained adjusted R² = 0.33 of pain-group variance at foot contact. Standardized regression coefficients were 0.513 for stride length, 0.516 for trunk rotation, and -0.403 for center of mass. Shoulder kinetic variables were not selected in this model.
paper.limitations: Pain may alter mechanics rather than mechanics causing pain; temporality is unresolved. Pain and pain-free groups differed in body weight, which was not included in the analysis. Small sample, variable-selection modeling, laboratory effort, one pitch type, and binary self-reported pain limit inference. No injury outcome or intervention test supports preventive exercise prescriptions.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the identified mechanics as assessment prompts when a pitcher reports pain, not as proven risk factors. Pair motion analysis with symptom location, workload, strength, medical evaluation, and prospective follow-up before changing technique.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use the identified mechanics as assessment prompts when a pitcher reports pain, not as proven risk factors. Pair motion analysis with symptom location, workload, strength, medical evaluation, and prospective follow-up before changing technique. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, use the identified mechanics as assessment prompts when a pitcher reports pain, not as proven risk factors. Pair motion analysis with symptom location, workload, strength, medical evaluation, and prospective follow-up before changing technique. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
